source_text:
quodsi animae maculas illi uitare uellent, haec mendacia potius et sacrilegia formidarent.,
Sed parua erat pro nobis domini nostri humilitas in nascendo; accessit etiam, ut mori pro mortalibus dignaretur. humiliauit enim se, factus subditus usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis, ne quisquam nostrum. etiamsi mortem posset non timere, aliquod genus mortis, quod homines ignominiosissimum arbitrantur, horreret. credimus itaque in eum, qui sub Pontio Pilato crucifixus est et sepultus. addendum enim erat iudicis nomen propter temporum cognitionem. sepultura uero illa cum creditur, fit recordatio noui monumenti, quod resurrecturo ad uitae nouitatem praeberet testimonium, sicut nascituro uterus uirginalis. nam sicut in illo monumento nullus alius mortuus sepultus est nec ante nec postea, sic in illo utero nec ante nec postea quidquam mortale conceptum est.
thought_title: The shameful death and the new tomb
orientation: Augustine has just argued that the Word could not be stained by a human body, and now turns to the humility of Christ's death and burial under Pontius Pilate.
pass_a_gloss: But if they wished to avoid stains of the soul, they would rather dread these lies and sacrileges. But the humility of our Lord in being born was small for us; it was added also, that he might deign to die for mortals. For he humbled himself, made subject all the way to death, even the death of the cross, lest any of us, even if he could not fear death, should shudder at some kind of death which men consider most disgraceful. Therefore we believe in him who was crucified under Pontius Pilate and was buried. For the name of the judge had to be added for the sake of knowledge of the times. But when that burial is believed, there comes about a remembrance of the new tomb, which would furnish testimony to the one about to rise to newness of life, just as the virginal womb to the one about to be born. For just as in that tomb no other dead person was buried, neither before nor after, so in that womb neither before nor after was anything mortal conceived.

choices.why: Keeps the gerund's force as the act of being born, matching the parallel 'resurrecturo' and 'nascituro' later in the section.

choices.english: made subject all the way to death
choices.why: Preserves the passive participle 'factus subditus' and the extent phrase 'usque ad' as a single movement toward death.
rejected: made obedient to the point of death

choices.english: even the death of the cross
choices.why: The 'autem' here intensifies rather than contrasts, so 'even' captures the climactic force better than 'but'.
rejected: but the death of the cross
and the death of the cross

choices.english: for the sake of knowledge of the times
choices.why: Literal rendering of the genitive plural 'temporum' and the noun 'cognitionem', avoiding the smoother but looser 'to date the event'.

choices.english: to the one about to rise to newness of life
choices.why: The future participle 'resurrecturo' is rendered as 'about to rise', and 'ad uitae nouitatem' keeps the prepositional phrase's direction.
rejected: to the one who would rise to new life
for the future resurrection to new life

choices.why: Keeps 'mortale' as a neuter substantive 'anything mortal' and the passive 'conceptum est', matching the tomb's 'no other dead person was buried'.

bible_refs.note: humiliauit enim se, factus subditus usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis

pass_b_english: But if they wanted to avoid stains on the soul, they should rather have dreaded these lies and sacrileges.

Yet our Lord's humility in being born was a small thing for our sake; he also deigned to die for mortals. For he humbled himself, made subject all the way to death, even the death of the cross (Philippians 2:8), so that none of us—even if we could manage not to fear death—would shudder at some kind of death that people consider most disgraceful.

We believe therefore in him who was crucified under Pontius Pilate and buried. The judge's name had to be added for the sake of knowledge of the times. And when that burial is believed, it calls to mind the new tomb, which would bear witness to the one about to rise to newness of life, just as the virgin's womb bore witness to the one about to be born. For just as no other dead person was buried in that tomb, neither before nor after, so in that womb nothing mortal was conceived, neither before nor after.

last_rejected.quote: a small thing for our sake
last_rejected.source_quote: parua erat pro nobis domini nostri humilitas in nascendo
last_rejected.why: 'parua erat' means 'was small/little,' but 'humilitas' is 'humility,' not 'a small thing.' The English makes it sound like the humility itself was small/trivial, when the Latin says his humility in being born was a small/lowly thing (i.e., humble). The sense is distorted: it's not that his humility was insignificant, but that it was lowly in manner.
last_rejected.fix: Yet our Lord's humility in being born was lowly for our sake
last_rejected.ruling: 'parua erat humilitas' = 'humility was small,' i.e., insufficient alone; English captures this adequately.

last_rejected.quote: he also deigned to die for mortals
last_rejected.source_quote: accessit etiam, ut mori pro mortalibus dignaretur
last_rejected.why: 'accessit etiam' means 'there was more besides/there was also added,' not 'he also deigned.' The structure indicates something further was added to the previous humility, not that Christ additionally deigned. The subject of 'dignaretur' is Christ, but 'accessit' is impersonal or refers to the addition of further humiliation.
last_rejected.fix: there was more besides: he deigned to die for mortals
last_rejected.ruling: 'accessit etiam' = 'there was added also'; English 'he also deigned' conveys same meaning without distortion.
